title: Nonogram Puzzle Checker
plainSentence: A picture-by-numbers (nonogram) maker that lets you draw a picture, get its clues, and check whether it can be solved without guessing.
pitch: Draw a picture on a small grid and the page writes the number clues around it, like a picture-by-numbers puzzle. It then solves the puzzle the way a person would, one row or column at a time, and reports whether the clues have exactly one answer and whether the whole grid falls out without guessing. If it does not, it shades the stuck squares and suggests a one-square change that repairs it; then you print the puzzle sheet and an answer page.
firstMinute: A 10 by 10 sample picture is already drawn with its clues written around it, and a slow replay is solving it pass by pass in colour. A verdict card reads something like 'One answer, no guessing needed, 6 passes, easy'. Click a single square to flip it and watch the verdict change, perhaps to 'Two answers' with the ambiguous squares shaded.
conceptsToLearn: A nonogram is a picture-by-numbers grid: each number says how long a run of filled squares is in that row or column.
whyNow: Timeless: anyone who makes puzzles for a book, a class or a friend hits the same trap, a puzzle that has one answer on paper but forces guessing. The page makes that visible in seconds.

purposeDetail.job: Turn a drawn picture into nonogram clues and prove, with visible working, whether the puzzle has exactly one answer and can be finished by row-and-column logic alone.
purposeDetail.audience: Puzzle makers, teachers, parents and hobbyists who want to design nonograms that are fair to solve, and solvers curious why a puzzle got stuck.

paywallEvidence.product: A paid no-guess nonogram toolkit sold through a small-seller storefront
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: The check that every accepted puzzle can be finished by row-and-column logic alone, plus a print-ready puzzle-book PDF with answer pages (seller claim; price not seen by the verifier and never shown on the page).

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free options already cover part of the job: a browser generator and an open-source library each verify line-solvability for puzzles they make, and a game's maker feature checks uniqueness. The remaining gap, not confirmed to be empty everywhere: a private in-browser checker for a picture you drew yourself that replays each solving pass, shades the stuck squares and proposes a one-square repair. The page names no product.
purposeDetail.oracle: OEIS A391619 (counts of n by n grids whose puzzle is unique and solvable by row-and-column logic alone): 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234 for sizes 0 to 4 and 24976511 for size 5. The self-test enumerates every grid up to 4 by 4 and compares; the 5 by 5 count is an optional background run. A small unique-but-stuck puzzle from a puzzle newsletter is a further case once its grid is copied correctly; its size was not confirmed.
purposeDetail.inputs: A picture drawn by clicking or dragging on a grid from 5 by 5 to 15 by 15 (20 by 20 under More), or pasted clue numbers; a sample picture is preloaded.
purposeDetail.outputs: Clue numbers, a verdict (no solution, several solutions, one solution needing guesses, or one solution reached by logic alone), a difficulty label from the pass count, the stuck squares, a suggested one-square repair, and exports: puzzle sheet and answer page as PNG, SVG and a print layout, plus a share link holding the grid.
purposeDetail.limits: Black-and-white nonograms only, 5 to 15 squares a side. Exhaustive checking of larger grids is capped and reported as 'could not decide' rather than guessed. Difficulty is a rough label from solving passes, not a verdict on how hard a person will find it. No photo import.

research.summary: Uniqueness and no-guess solvability are different properties. OEIS A391619 (submitted January 2026, on oeis.org) counts n by n grids whose puzzle is unique and solvable by analysing each row and column in isolation: 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511 for sizes 0 to 5. A puzzle newsletter (July 2025) and a forum thread agree on 24,976,511 for 5 by 5 and give the same definition. A seller's own listing says its paid toolkit accepts only puzzles finished by line logic and that most generators check nothing or only uniqueness (seller claim). Free line-solvability checks exist inside a browser generator and an open-source library, so the page must win on checking a hand-drawn picture, showing each pass and proposing a repair. A larger unique-solution count for 5 by 5 (25,309,575) is relayed by a newsletter and a commenter and stays unconfirmed. The verifier recomputed sizes 1 to 4 with an independent brute-force line solver and got 2, 14, 384 and 51234, matching OEIS (a regression check, not an oracle).

facts.claim: A seller's own listing offers a paid no-guess nonogram toolkit that accepts a puzzle only if working one row or column at a time, filling only forced squares, finishes the grid, and says most generators check nothing or only uniqueness (seller claim, never shown on the page).

A nonogram can have exactly one solution and still not be solvable by row-and-column logic alone: a puzzle newsletter (July 2025) defines logically solvable as unique plus line-solvable and shows a unique puzzle where line work gets stuck; OEIS A391619 uses the same definition for the puzzles it counts.

OEIS A391619 lists 1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511 for n by n grids with n from 0 to 5 whose puzzle is unique and solvable by analysing each row and column in isolation; of the 33,554,432 possible 5 by 5 grids, 24,976,511 qualify.

The OEIS entry defines the counted puzzles as solvable by iteratively analysing each row and column in isolation without guessing or backtracking, and credits Batenburg and Kosters, whose paper studies a subclass of nonograms solvable by sequences of local reasoning steps. Cheap line passes plus a capped search therefore suit an in-browser checker.

Free line-solvability checks already exist for generated puzzles: a browser generator verifies each puzzle with a line-logic solver from a blank board, and an open-source Dart library offers a line-solvable check. Whether any free tool checks a hand-drawn picture with a replay and a repair suggestion is not confirmed.

Reported, unconfirmed: a puzzle newsletter and a forum commenter give 25,309,575 as the number of uniquely solvable 5 by 5 grids (OEIS A242876), a gap of 333,064 above the line-solvable count; the A242876 entry itself was seen only with an approximate 75 percent figure.

inspirations: level editors with a built-in playtest

design.coreLoop: Input, output, refine: draw or edit squares, see clues and the verdict update instantly, replay the solver pass by pass, apply the suggested repair or redraw, then export when the verdict is green.
sophisticationHooks: Pass-coloured replay: each square is tinted by the pass in which logic fixed it, so the rating is visible, not just a number
Stuck squares shaded when logic stops, plus an exhaustive count of answers up to two with a node cap and an honest 'could not decide'
One-square repair search: try flipping each square and report flips that make the puzzle unique and line-solvable
Self-test panel that enumerates every grid up to 4 by 4 and checks the counts against published sequences
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: drawing grid (5, 10, 15), clue generator, line solver with pass replay, depth-first answer counter with a node cap, difficulty label, single-flip repair search in a worker (default sizes up to 10, 15 on request), SVG and print-layout export, share link in the page address, self-test over all grids up to 4 by 4 plus the optional 5 by 5 run. Cut: 20 by 20 grids, PNG export, coloured nonograms, photo import, puzzle packs, accounts.
risks: The paywall claim rests on one seller listing (its own page, so it passes the primary-source rule, but it is a marketing claim with no independent review and the price was not seen); it never goes on the page and the page names no product.

The 5 by 5 uniquely-solvable count 25,309,575 and the 333,064 gap are unconfirmed (relayed by a newsletter and a commenter); the page leaves them out or shows them as 'as of 2026-10-14, per a puzzle newsletter'.

The OEIS entry was seen in search results and not opened (oeis.org was not fetchable); sizes 1 to 4 were also recomputed by the verifier with an independent brute-force solver and match, and the 5 by 5 value agrees with a newsletter and a forum thread.

The self-test needs 8 known-answer cases from named sources: counts for sizes 0 to 5 give 6 and the newsletter's stuck example needs its grid copied exactly (its size was not confirmed); the spec must add definition-based cases labelled as such, or report fewer named-source cases honestly.

Free line-solvability checks exist inside a generator and a library, so the page must not claim to be the only no-guess check; it states only what it does (checks a drawn picture, shows each pass, proposes a repair, works offline and privately).

NP-hardness of nonogram solving is a widely cited background fact that was not re-seen this run; the page says only that exhaustive answer counting is capped and reports 'could not decide' when the cap is hit.
Brute-force over all 33 million 5 by 5 grids may be slow in a browser; keep sizes 0 to 4 automatic and make the 5 by 5 run an optional worker with a progress bar.

A drawn grid has many focusable squares; it must be one composite widget with a single tab stop and arrow-key movement so the first screen stays within 8 controls and the primary button stays visible at 1280x650.
Difficulty by pass count is a rough proxy; the page says so rather than claiming a human rating.

verification.notes: The key count and definition are on the OEIS entry itself and agree with a newsletter and a forum thread; sizes 1 to 4 were recomputed by an independent brute-force solver. The seller claim is its own page; the larger unique count and the free-gap claim stay unconfirmed, and two free line-solvability checks for generated puzzles exist.
